name: Vitruvius
credit: The Vitruvian Man, drawn by Leonardo da Vinci to illustrate Vitruvius’s account of human proportion (c. 1492; Gallerie dell’Accademia, Venice; photograph by Luc Viatour). An illustration of his theme, shown because no portrait of Vitruvius survives · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Marcus Vitruvius Pollio was a Roman architect and military engineer of the late Republic and the age of Augustus. He served under Julius Caesar, probably as a builder and maker of siege engines, and was afterwards given a pension by Augustus through the good offices of the emperor’s sister Octavia. Little else is known of his life, and even his birthplace and the dates of his birth and death are uncertain.

His De architectura, written in Latin about 30–15 BC and addressed to Augustus, is the only complete treatise on architecture to survive from antiquity. In ten books it treats the training of the architect, the founding and planning of cities, building materials, temples and the orders, public and private buildings, water, sundials and clocks, and machines of peace and war. The treatise shaped Renaissance architecture, and its passage on the proportions of the human body inspired Leonardo’s famous drawing. The English version given here is by Morris Hicky Morgan (1914).
